title: Reading Metrics and Logs Like an SRE
intro: Monitoring isn't just dashboards — it's knowing which question to ask the data. Let's practice the basics: checking if something is up, querying a rate, and searching logs.

steps.prompt: Query Prometheus to check if the 'checkout-service' target is up.
steps.explanation: A value of "1" means Prometheus successfully scraped it last time; "0" means the target is down or unreachable.
steps.why: You could check the same thing visually in the Prometheus web UI, but hitting the HTTP API directly with curl is what you'd actually do inside a script or a quick terminal check without switching to a browser.

steps.prompt: In the Prometheus UI, what PromQL would show the 5-minute request rate for http_requests_total?
steps.fake_output: (Graph showing requests/sec over time, per label combination)
steps.explanation: rate() is essential for counters — raw counter values only ever go up, so you always wrap them in rate() to get something meaningful like requests/sec.
steps.why: Just graphing http_requests_total directly would show an ever-climbing line that resets to 0 on every restart — completely useless for spotting a traffic drop. rate() converts that raw ever-increasing counter into a per-second value that actually reflects what's happening right now.

steps.prompt: Now write a PromQL query for the 95th percentile request latency.
steps.explanation: p95/p99 matter more than averages — a slow 5% of requests can be a real user-facing problem an average completely hides.
steps.why: An average latency query would be simpler to write, but it's exactly what hides the problem you're usually looking for — a handful of genuinely painful slow requests get smoothed away by thousands of fast ones. histogram_quantile is the standard way to surface that tail instead of averaging it out.

steps.prompt: Search recent logs for any 500 errors in the last hour.
steps.explanation: Combining a time-scoped log fetch with grep is one of the single most common on-call actions there is.
steps.why: journalctl is for a service running directly on a host (via systemd); kubectl logs is for one running as a pod — same underlying instinct (get logs, scope by time, filter with grep), just a different command depending on where the thing actually runs.
